account: VOA Learning English reported on 16 November 2022, drawing on Associated Press coverage, that two U.S. studies had quantified the effect of front crash prevention. The Partnership for Analytics Research in Traffic Safety (PARTS) is a collaboration between automakers and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. It examined more than 12 million police-reported crashes in 13 states involving 93 vehicle models from 2015 to 2020. It found that front-to-rear crashes were reduced by 49% when the striking vehicle had both forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking. Injury crashes were down 53%. Stellantis executive Tim Czapp of the PARTS board was quoted. The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) used police-reported crashes in 25 states from 2017 to 2020. It found that automatic emergency braking reduced rear-end crash rates for pickups by 43%. IIHS researcher Jessica Cicchino urged automakers to fit every pickup with the feature. These are different studies from the 2017 IIHS analysis. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor lists the coverage as an aggregate benefit. The 2022 PARTS report itself is not among the sources. Jessica Cicchino published the IIHS pickup study in Traffic Injury Prevention on 28 February 2023. In its main analysis she found a 34% lower risk of rear-end-striking crashes with automatic emergency braking. In its final rule of 9 May 2024, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration found that automatic emergency braking had reduced injuries and saved lives. The rule requires automatic emergency braking on all new light vehicles from September 2029. On 6 January 2025 PARTS published a second study, on model years 2015–2023. It again measured a 49% reduction in front-to-rear crashes for vehicles equipped with automatic emergency braking. Effectiveness rose from 46% for 2015–2017 models to 52% for 2021–2023 models.

ai_role.statement: Camera and radar perception detects a vehicle ahead and triggers warnings and braking. The studies isolate the systems' effect by comparing crash rates of equipped and unequipped vehicles; IIHS used quasi-induced exposure, which compares a vehicle's rear-end strikes with being struck in the rear, and Poisson models of crashes per registered vehicle year. The estimates credit the whole warning and braking system and do not separate the perception software from the brakes or from driver response to the warning.

fields.account: VOA Learning English reported on 16 November 2022, drawing on Associated Press coverage, that two U.S. studies had quantified the effect of front crash prevention. The Partnership for Analytics Research in Traffic Safety (PARTS) is a collaboration between automakers and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. It examined more than 12 million police-reported crashes in 13 states involving 93 vehicle models from 2015 to 2020. It found that front-to-rear crashes were reduced by 49% when the striking vehicle had both forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking. Injury crashes were down 53%. Stellantis executive Tim Czapp of the PARTS board was quoted. The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) used police-reported crashes in 25 states from 2017 to 2020. It found that automatic emergency braking reduced rear-end crash rates for pickups by 43%. IIHS researcher Jessica Cicchino urged automakers to fit every pickup with the feature. These are different studies from the 2017 IIHS analysis. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor lists the coverage as an aggregate benefit. The 2022 PARTS report itself is not among the sources. Jessica Cicchino published the IIHS pickup study in Traffic Injury Prevention on 28 February 2023. In its main analysis she found a 34% lower risk of rear-end-striking crashes with automatic emergency braking. In its final rule of 9 May 2024, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration found that automatic emergency braking had reduced injuries and saved lives. The rule requires automatic emergency braking on all new light vehicles from September 2029. On 6 January 2025 PARTS published a second study, on model years 2015–2023. It again measured a 49% reduction in front-to-rear crashes for vehicles equipped with automatic emergency braking. Effectiveness rose from 46% for 2015–2017 models to 52% for 2021–2023 models.
